category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 1 — HAVE TO VS MUST | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Both have to and must express obligation, duty, or necessity. The key difference is: 'have to' represents an external obligation (e.g., your boss, company, or law), while 'must' represents an internal or personal obligation (e.g., a self-imposed duty or conscious decision). For laws and instructions, we mostly use 'have to'.
exampleText:
• Boss / Workplace Instruction (have to): My manager told me I have to finish this presentation before tomorrow's meeting.
• Company Policy (have to): All employees have to submit their weekly timesheets by Friday evening.
• Law / Official Regulation (have to): Drivers have to stop when the traffic light turns red.
• Self-Imposed Duty (must): I must call my mother tonight because I miss her.
• Conscious / Internal Duty (must): I feel I must buy fresh vegetables and cook a healthy meal tonight.
• Boss / Job: I have to complete this presentation before tomorrow's meeting — my boss needs it.
• Company: I have to follow the company's dress code during work hours.
• Law: You have to stop at a red light. (Self-aware: You must obey traffic signals — it's the right thing to do.)
• Self-Imposed Obligation: I must buy vegetables and cook a healthy dinner tonight (no one is forcing me).
• Conscious / Personal Duty: I must wake up early every day to stay disciplined.
• Form across tenses (have to): I have to work. → I had to work. → I will have to work.
• Form across tenses (must — stays the same): I must work. She must have paid the taxes. We must win the match.
speechPrompt: I must buy fresh vegetables and cook a healthy meal tonight.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 2 — USE OF 'HAVE TO' AND 'MUST' IN ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: Must and have to express an obligation or responsibility. In negative sentences, 'must not' (mustn't) means it is prohibited, while 'don't have to' means it is not necessary. Note that 'must' has no past or future form; we use 'had to' for the past and 'will have to' for the future.
exampleText:
• Affirmative Obligation (have to): You have to wear a seat belt when driving on the highway.
• Negative Prohibition (must not / mustn't): You must not leave your homework incomplete.
• Lack of Necessity (don't have to): You don't have to wear a tie to work on Casual Friday.
• Past Obligation (had to): Yesterday, I had to work late to complete the quarterly audit.
• Future Obligation (will have to): Next week, we will have to submit our project proposals.
• Self-decided / Internal: I must write this email — I feel it's necessary, no one told me to.
• External instruction (boss/other person): I have to write this email — my manager asked me to send it.
• Company obligation: I have to submit my timesheet by Friday; it's company policy.
• Law: I have to renew my driving license before it expires.
• Self-imposed: I must start exercising — I've decided this is important for my health.
speechPrompt: You must not leave your homework incomplete.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 3 — ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON - DIFFERENCE BETWEEN HAVE TO, OUGHT TO & SUPPOSED TO
explanation: 'Have to' or 'must' means you have no choice. 'Supposed to' indicates an obligation or a rule that you are expected to follow, but you still have a choice. 'Ought to' is used for advice or suggestions and is not as strong as 'have to' or 'supposed to'.
exampleText:
• No Choice (have to / must): I have to submit the financial reports tomorrow morning.
• Expected Rule with Choice (supposed to): We are supposed to submit the reports by tomorrow, but we can request an extension.
• Advice / Suggestion (ought to): You ought to get some sleep before your early flight.
• Have to (law): You have to wear a seatbelt while driving.
• Have to (boss): I have to attend the client meeting; my manager scheduled it.
• Ought to (moral duty): You ought to apologize to her — it's the right thing to do.
• Supposed to (arrangement/expectation): I was supposed to call him at 5 PM, but I forgot.
• Supposed to (rule): Students are supposed to submit assignments online.
speechPrompt: We are supposed to submit the reports by tomorrow.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 4 — DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ‘HAVE TO’, SUPPOSE TO & OUGHT TO
explanation: Both 'have to' and 'must' express obligation, whereas 'supposed to' means an expected behavior or rule. 'Ought to' is used for suggestions and moral duties where you have a choice. In negative sentences and questions, 'ought to' is rarely used.
exampleText:
• Obligation (have to): I have to pay my property taxes by the end of the month.
• Expected Behavior (supposed to): You are supposed to keep your phone on silent during the presentation.
• Moral Duty / Suggestion (ought to): We ought to help our elderly neighbors carry their heavy groceries.
• Negative Expected Rule (not supposed to): You are not supposed to talk loudly inside a hospital.
• Have to (company): All employees have to complete the security training by month-end.
• Have to (law): You have to pay import duty on that item.
• Supposed to (plan/expectation): The train is supposed to arrive at 6 PM.
• Supposed to (rule not followed): He was supposed to lock the office, but he left it open.
• Ought to (sensible advice): You ought to save some money every month.
speechPrompt: You are not supposed to talk loudly in a hospital.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 5 — ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON - USING ‘MUST’ CORRECTLY IN SENTENCES AND QUESTIONS.
explanation: Must is a modal auxiliary verb and always takes the base form of the verb. It can express personal obligation ('I must study'), logical certainty ('This must be the right address'), or a strong recommendation ('You must visit that new place'). In questions, we often prefer 'Do you have to?' instead of 'Must you?'.
exampleText:
• Personal Obligation: I must finish reading this textbook before my exam on Monday.
• Logical Certainty: He has been working in the garden all afternoon, so he must be tired.
• Strong Recommendation: You must visit that new Italian restaurant downtown—the food is incredible.
• Question Form (Do you have to?): Do you have to leave so early, or can you stay for coffee?
• Conscious / self-imposed duty: I must finish reading this book before the exam.
• Boss-driven necessity expressed as internal resolve: I must impress the client during tomorrow's presentation.
• Law-related necessity (formal must): Citizens must carry valid identification at all times.
• Certainty / deduction: She must be at home — her car is in the driveway.
• Question (preferring have to over must): Do I have to attend the meeting? (rather than "Must I attend the meeting?")
speechPrompt: Being confident in an interview is a must.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 6 — USING ‘MUSTN'T’ AND ‘NEEDN'T’ CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Mustn't' means you are not allowed to do something (prohibition/restriction), whereas 'needn't' means it is not necessary to do something (you have a choice, it's optional).
exampleText:
• Prohibition / Restriction (mustn't): You mustn't tell anyone our secret company plans.
• Lack of Necessity / Optional (needn't): You needn't carry physical documents with you since everything is saved online.
• Prohibition (law/rule): You mustn't park here — it's a no-parking zone.
• Prohibition (self-imposed discipline): I mustn't skip my workout this week.
• No obligation (optional task): You needn't carry the documents; they're not required today.
• No obligation (boss/workplace): You needn't come to the office on Sunday.
• Contrast pair: You mustn't lose these papers (they're important) vs. You needn't lose sleep over it (it's not a big deal either way).
speechPrompt: You needn't carry the documents with you today.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 7 — USING 'NEED' CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Need' can act as a main verb (meaning 'require' or 'necessity') and takes the regular verb forms ('needs to', 'needed to'). It can also act as an auxiliary verb in negative sentences ('need not') and questions ('Need we wait?').
exampleText:
• Main Verb (need to): I need to buy some groceries for dinner tonight.
• Modal Verb (needn't): You needn't worry about dinner reservations; I already booked a table.
• Noun Form (in need of): The local shelter is in urgent need of warm blankets.
• Main verb: I need some new winter clothes.
• Main verb, third person: She needs to talk to him now.
• Auxiliary verb, negative: You need not ask my permission.
• Auxiliary verb, question: Need we wait any longer?
• Past ("needn't have"): We needn't have waited for them — they never showed up.
• Noun (necessity): Food, clothing, and shelter are basic human needs.
• Need vs. desire: A need is a necessity (I need food); a desire is just a want (I desire a Ferrari).
speechPrompt: You needn't have lost your temper.

title: Lesson 8 — ALL USES OF SHOULD IN ENGLISH | MASTER MODAL VERBS
explanation: 'Should' is used to give advice/recommendations ('You should see a doctor'), express moral duty/obligation ('You should keep promises'), or express expectations ('The package should arrive tomorrow'). 'Should have' is used for past regrets or criticism.
exampleText:
• Giving Advice: You should see a doctor if your fever doesn't go down.
• Expecting Probability: The train should arrive in about ten minutes.
• Negative Advice (shouldn't): You shouldn't drink coffee right before going to bed.
• Past Regret (should have): I should have studied harder for the final exam.
speechPrompt: I should have studied harder for the exam.

title: Lesson 9 — ALL USES OF 'SHOULD' IN ENGLISH | FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: 'Should' is a modal verb that does not change with subject ('I should', 'He should'). It is used to suggest actions or predict likely outcomes based on facts or patterns.
exampleText:
• Recommendation: You should try the roasted salmon at this café.
• Logical Expectation: They left an hour ago, so they should be here soon.
• Criticism / Past Regret (should have): You should have warned me about the heavy traffic.
speechPrompt: I don't think you should spend your salary online.

title: Lesson 10 — USING ' SHOULD ' IN DIFFERENT WAYS - ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'should' for advising, recommendations, or predicting probabilities. In negative sentences, 'shouldn't' is used to advise against something. Use 'should have' with past participle to express regret.
exampleText:
• Future Expectation (should): He should reach the office any minute now.
• Negative Suggestion (shouldn't): You shouldn't stay up late watching television.
• Past Regret (should have): I shouldn't have shouted at you during the meeting yesterday.
speechPrompt: I shouldn't have shouted at you yesterday.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 11 — MASTER ALL USES OF THE MODAL VERB 'COULD' | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' but can also express present possibility or polite requests. We use 'could have' for past possibilities or missed opportunities.
exampleText:
• Past Ability (could): When I was younger, I could run ten miles without stopping.
• Present Possibility (could): It could rain later this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
• Polite Request (Could you...): Could you please pass me the water pitcher?
• Past Possibility / Missed Opportunity (could have): I could have won the race, but I tripped near the finish line.
speechPrompt: I could have won the race, but I gave up.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 12 — ALL USES OF ‘COULD’ IN PRESENT, PAST & FUTURE TENSES
explanation: 'Could' is used for past abilities ('I could swim'), future possibilities ('It could rain'), and polite requests. Do not use 'could' for specific one-time past achievements; use 'was able to' instead.
exampleText:
• Present Possibility: We could eat dinner outdoors if the weather stays warm.
• Past General Ability: In high school, she could play the piano effortlessly.
• Future Suggestion: We could go on a road trip this upcoming weekend.
• Conditional Sentence: We could travel the world if we won the lottery.
speechPrompt: Yesterday I couldn't lift the sofa by myself.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 13 — MODAL VERBS - CAN AND COULD - ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Can' is used for present ability or informal requests and permission. 'Could' is used for past ability or formal/polite requests. Always follow both with the base form of the verb.
exampleText:
• Present Ability (can): He can speak three languages fluently.
• Past Ability (could): She could swim across the lake when she was ten.
• Informal Permission (can): Can I use your phone for a quick call?
• Polite Request (could): Could I borrow your book for a day, please?
speechPrompt: Could I borrow your book for a day, please?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 14 — DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WILL VS WOULD | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'will' for real, definite, or promised future situations with high certainty. Use 'would' for imaginary, hypothetical, polite, or past habits/refusals.
exampleText:
• Certain Future / Promise (will): I will pick you up at six o'clock sharp.
• Hypothetical Situation (would): I would pick you up if I had a car available.
• Past Habitual Action (would): Every summer, we would visit our grandparents in the countryside.
• Polite Offer / Request (would): Would you like a cup of hot tea?
speechPrompt: I would pick you up if I had a car.

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 15 — ALL USES OF THE MODAL VERB 'WOULD' - FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: 'Would' is a versatile modal verb used for conditionals ('If I won, I would buy a car'), future-in-the-past ('They said they would come'), past habits ('Every morning she would run'), and polite requests ('Would you mind?').
exampleText:
• Conditional Statement: If I had more free time, I would study photography.
• Polite Request (Would you mind...): Would you mind closing the window, please?
• Preferences (would rather): I would rather stay home than go to a crowded party.
• Past Habit: Grandfather would tell us stories by the fireplace every evening.
speechPrompt: Would you mind passing me the salt, please?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 16 — ALL USES OF MODAL VERB 'WOULD' | ENGLISH GRAMMAR PRACTICE
explanation: 'Would' adds politeness and diplomacy in questions and statements. It contracts to 'I'd' for subjects and can express preferences like 'would rather'.
exampleText:
• Offering Help (Shall I...): Shall I carry those heavy bags to your car?
• Initiating Action (Shall we...): Shall we begin the presentation now?
• Future Prediction / Outcome (Will we...): Will we arrive at the airport on time?
speechPrompt: I'd rather take a cab than walk to the office.

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 17 — 'WILL I/WE' OR 'SHALL I/WE' IN QUESTIONS (FUTURE) - WHICH ONE IS CORRECT?
explanation: Use 'shall I/we' when offering to do something or initiating an action. Use 'will I/we' when asking about future outcomes where you are not offering or controlling the action.
exampleText:
• Offer / Suggestion (Shall I / Shall we): Shall I turn on the air conditioner?
• Future Event Inquiry (Will I / Will we): Will we get a certificate after completing the course?
speechPrompt: Will I recover soon from this cold, doctor?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 18 — USING THE AUXILIARY VERB - WOULD - FREE ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'would' for past habits, indirect speech 'will' conversion, conditional sentences, or expressing preferences with 'would rather'.
exampleText:
• Past Habitual Action: I would read a lot during my college days.
• Indirect Speech Conversion: He promised that he would send the email.
• Preference (would rather): I would rather drink tea than coffee.
speechPrompt: Would you mind helping me with my project?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 19 — USING 'WILL' - GRAMMAR ESL LESSON
explanation: Use 'will' to talk about certain future events, beliefs with words like 'probably/maybe', decisions made at the moment of speaking, or promises.
exampleText:
• Spontaneous Decision: It's cold; I will close the window.
• Future Prediction with Belief: The sun will rise over there tomorrow morning.
• Promise / Commitment: I will always support your dreams.
speechPrompt: Perhaps we will meet again someday.

title: Lesson 20 — USING MAY AND MIGHT - BASIC ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'may' for formal permissions ('May I leave?') and higher possibilities. Use 'might' for smaller or less likely possibilities.
exampleText:
• Formal Permission (may): May I leave the conference room early today?
• High Possibility (may): The store may close early because of the storm.
• Lower / Slight Possibility (might): I might visit my aunt this weekend if I finish my work.
speechPrompt: I might have forgotten my keys at the cafe.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 21 — MAY HAVE VS MIGHT HAVE VS MUST HAVE | PAST MODAL VERBS
explanation: 'May have' and 'might have' show around 50% or less certainty about a past event. 'Must have' shows high logical certainty based on strong evidence or facts.
exampleText:
• Around 50% Certainty (may have): She may have gone to the central library.
• Slight Possibility (might have): I might have left my keys in the office, but I am not sure.
• High Logical Certainty (must have): He must have left his phone at home because he isn't answering.
speechPrompt: He must have left his phone at home.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 22 — MODAL VERBS OF THE PAST – MAY HAVE, MIGHT HAVE, MUST HAVE — WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE?
explanation: 'May have' is more formal; 'might have' is more common in spoken English. 'Must have' expresses an educated guess based on logic or results.
exampleText:
• Formal Possibility (may have): The company may have experienced financial delays.
• Spoken Possibility (might have): We might have taken the wrong turn at the intersection.
• Deduction / Strong Evidence (must have): The ground is soaked; it must have rained heavily last night.
speechPrompt: She must have been crying; her eyes are red.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 23 — PAST MODAL VERBS – COULD HAVE, SHOULD HAVE, WOULD HAVE, MIGHT HAVE, MUST HAVE
explanation: Past modal verbs use 'modal + have + past participle'. 'Could have' is missed possibility; 'should have' is past regret; 'would have' is imaginary past outcome.
exampleText:
• Missed Possibility (could have): We could have won the match if we had practiced more.
• Past Regret / Obligation (should have): I should have double-checked the flight times before leaving.
• Imaginary Past Outcome (would have): I would have attended the wedding, but I fell ill.
• Slight Past Guess (might have): They might have forgotten about our dinner meeting.
• Strong Logical Conclusion (must have): She must have passed the test easily because she studied for weeks.
speechPrompt: I should have studied harder for the exam.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 24 — USING SHOULD, COULD AND WOULD HAVE DONE CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Should have done' implies a missed obligation or regret. 'Could have done' means a choice or possibility you decided not to take. 'Would have done' means you wanted to but were stopped by circumstances.
exampleText:
• Missed Obligation / Regret (should have done): You should have done your homework before playing games.
• Untaken Opportunity / Choice (could have done): We could have done the tour by bike, but we chose to walk.
• Blocked Intention (would have done): I would have done the cooking, but we ran out of gas.
speechPrompt: I would have completed my project, but there was no electricity.

title: Lesson 25 — ALL USES OF BEEN AND BEING | FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Been' is the past participle of be, used with has/have/had. 'Being' is the present participle, used with am/is/are/was/were for temporary behaviors or passive continuous tenses.
exampleText:
• Past Participle Experience (been): I have been to London twice in the past three years.
• Temporary Behavior (being): You are being overly dramatic about a minor issue.
• Passive Continuous Action (being): The broken car is being repaired at the mechanic shop.
speechPrompt: You are being rude to her right now.

title: Lesson 26 — MASTER ALL USES OF BEING
explanation: 'Being' can express temporary behavior, passive voice ('The car is being washed'), temporary emotional state, or act as a gerund/noun ('I love being a teacher').
exampleText:
• Temporary Behavior: Why are you being so quiet this morning?
• Passive Voice Action: The road is currently being resurfaced.
• Gerund / Noun Role: I truly enjoy being a mentor to young students.
speechPrompt: Thank you for being so patient with us.

title: Lesson 27 — MASTER ALL USES OF BEEN
explanation: 'Been' has eight main uses, including travel/experiences ('I've been to Japan'), states/conditions, ongoing actions, visits, and passive perfect voice.
exampleText:
• Travel & Life Experiences: Have you ever been to Hawaii?
• State / Condition Over Time: She has been ill for three days.
• Ongoing Duration in Present Perfect: We have been waiting for the bus since eight o'clock.
speechPrompt: I've been busy with work all week.

title: Lesson 28 — HOW TO USE BEING IN ENGLISH? – ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'being' for temporary action or behavior followed by an adjective, in passive voice, or as a replacement for 'since', 'as', or 'because'. Do not use 'being' to show simple emotions like 'I was being upset'.
exampleText:
• Temporary Behavior + Adjective: He is being foolish by ignoring the doctor's advice.
• Passive Action in Progress: The new building is being constructed downtown.
• Cause / Reason Replacement: Being tired after the long drive, she went straight to bed.
speechPrompt: Being a friend of the actor, I am invited to parties.

title: Lesson 29 — WHEN TO USE HAVE & HAVING? GRAMMAR DOUBT SOLVED!
explanation: Use 'have' for permanent possession, relationships, or state. Use 'having' for ongoing temporary actions like meals, events, or short experiences.
exampleText:
• Permanent Possession / State (have): They have a lovely summer home near the ocean.
• Ongoing Temporary Experience (having): We are having lunch at a sidewalk terrace.
• Events & Meetings (having): Our company is having an annual meeting next Tuesday.
speechPrompt: We are having a meeting at the office.

title: Lesson 30 — WHEN TO USE HAD HAD IN ONE SENTENCE? ​​ PAST PERFECT TENSE MADE SIMPLE
explanation: 'Had had' is correct in the past perfect tense. The first 'had' is the auxiliary verb; the second 'had' is the past participle meaning experienced, possessed, or eaten.
exampleText:
• Had Had (Auxiliary Had + Past Participle Had): By the time the guests arrived, we had already had our dinner.
• Past Perfect Experience: She felt confident because she had had extensive training prior to the test.
speechPrompt: She had had a headache before she took medicine.

title: Lesson 31 — HOW TO USE ‘HAVE HAD’ CORRECTLY IN ONE SENTENCE?
explanation: 'Have had' is the present perfect tense of 'have'. Use it to show continuous possession from past to present, or completed actions within a current time frame.
exampleText:
• Present Perfect Continuous Possession (have had): I have had this car for over ten years.
• Recent Completed Experience: We have had a wonderful afternoon spending time together.
speechPrompt: She has had a headache since yesterday.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 32 — Auxiliary Verbs: 'Do' and 'Does' in Questions & Negatives
explanation: Use 'do' with I, you, we, they and 'does' with he, she, it to form present simple questions and negative statements. Remember that after 'does' or 'doesn't', the main verb returns to its base form (e.g., 'Does she like...?' not 'likes').
exampleText:
• Question with I / You / We / They (do): Do you enjoy listening to classical music?
• Question with He / She / It (does): Does she live near the city center?
• Negative Statement (don't / doesn't): He doesn't eat spicy food.
speechPrompt: Do you prefer tea or coffee in the morning?

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 33 — Auxiliary Verb 'Did' in Past Simple Tense
explanation: Use 'did' for all subjects (I, you, he, she, we, they) when forming questions or negatives in the past simple. Once 'did' or 'didn't' is used, the main verb stays in its base form.
exampleText:
• Past Simple Question (did): Did you visit your grandparents over the weekend?
• Past Simple Negative (didn't + base verb): They didn't finish the project on time.
speechPrompt: I didn't hear the phone ring during the meeting.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 34 — Auxiliary 'Have' & 'Has' in Present Perfect Sentences
explanation: Use 'have' (I, you, we, they) or 'has' (he, she, it) combined with the past participle (V3) to form the present perfect tense, describing actions with present relevance.
exampleText:
• Present Perfect with I/You/We/They (have + V3): We have already submitted the revised proposal.
• Present Perfect with He/She/It (has + V3): She has completed her master's thesis.
speechPrompt: We have finished all our assignments for this week.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 35 — Auxiliary 'Be' (Am/Is/Are/Was/Were) in Continuous Tenses
explanation: The auxiliary verb 'be' combines with present participles (-ing) to create continuous tenses, showing ongoing actions in the present or past.
exampleText:
• Present Continuous (am/is/are + -ing): They are discussing the new strategy in the room.
• Past Continuous (was/were + -ing): I was reading a book when the electricity went out.
speechPrompt: I am currently preparing for my English fluency test.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 36 — Emphatic 'Do', 'Does', and 'Did' for Strong Assertions
explanation: You can place 'do', 'does', or 'did' before a main verb in affirmative sentences to add strong emphasis or contrast a previous doubt (e.g., 'I do care about your progress').
exampleText:
• Emphatic Assertion (do): I do care deeply about your future success!
• Emphatic Assertion (does): She does work hard, even if she stays quiet.
• Emphatic Assertion in Past (did): We did lock the door before leaving the house.
speechPrompt: She does know how to solve this difficult problem.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 37 — Present Perfect Simple: Life Experiences & Recent Actions
explanation: Present Perfect Simple connects past events with the present moment. Use it for life experiences ('I have visited Japan'), accomplishments, or recent events without specifying an exact past time.
exampleText:
• Life Experience: I have visited France three times in my life.
• Recent Accomplishment / Action: He has just finished painting the dining room.
speechPrompt: Have you ever traveled abroad on your own?

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 38 — Present Perfect Continuous: Ongoing Unfinished Actions
explanation: Formed with 'have/has been + verb-ing', this tense emphasizes the duration or ongoing nature of an action that started in the past and continues into the present.
exampleText:
• Ongoing Unfinished Action: She has been studying medicine for four years.
• Recent Process with Present Effect: It has been raining all morning, so the ground is wet.
speechPrompt: It has been raining continuously since morning.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 39 — Present Perfect Simple vs Present Perfect Continuous
explanation: Use Present Perfect Simple when focusing on completion, result, or quantity ('I have written three letters'). Use Present Perfect Continuous when focusing on duration, process, or activity ('I have been writing all morning').
exampleText:
• Focus on Completion / Quantity (Simple): I have written three client reports today.
• Focus on Duration / Process (Continuous): I have been writing client reports all morning.
speechPrompt: I have been calling him, but he hasn't answered yet.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 40 — Past Perfect Simple ('Had Done') for Earlier Past Actions
explanation: Past Perfect Simple ('had + V3') indicates an action that happened before another past event or a specific point in the past.
exampleText:
• Earlier Past Action (Past Perfect): When we arrived at the cinema, the movie had already started.
• Sequence of Past Events: She had saved enough money before she bought her first apartment.
speechPrompt: She had finished her work before the manager asked for it.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)

title: Lesson 50 — Stative Verbs: Why Certain Verbs Don't Take '-ing'

title: Lesson 51 — Dynamic vs Stative Uses of Verbs (Think, Have, See)

title: Lesson 52 — Expressing Future: 'Will' vs 'Going To' vs Present Continuous

• Spontaneous Decision / Prediction (will): I am thirsty; I will buy a bottle of water.

title: Lesson 53 — Future Time Clauses: Present Simple After 'When', 'If', 'As Soon As'

title: Lesson 58 — Zero & First Conditionals: Facts & Real Possibilities

title: Lesson 59 — Second Conditional: Hypothetical Present & Advice

title: Lesson 60 — Third Conditional: Unreal Past & Regrets

title: Lesson 61 — Coordinating Conjunctions: FANBOYS Rules
explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So) join equal clauses or words. Always place a comma before them when connecting independent clauses.
exampleText:
• For (reason / cause): He bought a warm jacket, for the mountain air was chilly.
• And (addition): I like drinking tea, and she prefers coffee.
• Nor (negative choice): He doesn't eat meat, nor does he drink dairy milk.
• But (contrast): I wanted to go for a walk, but it began to rain heavily.
• Or (alternative): You can take the bus, or you can order a taxi.
• Yet (unexpected contrast): He was completely exhausted, yet he finished the marathon.
• So (result / consequence): It was getting dark, so we decided to return home.

title: Lesson 62 — Subordinating Conjunctions: Reason & Cause
explanation: Use subordinating conjunctions like because, since, as, and due to the fact that to introduce clauses explaining reasons.
exampleText:
• because (direct cause): We stayed indoors because the weather was stormy.
• since (known reason / cause): Since it was a public holiday, all banks were closed.
• as (formal cause): As the meeting room was full, we moved to the auditorium.
• due to the fact that (formal written reason): Due to the fact that flights were canceled, we stayed an extra night.

title: Lesson 63 — Correlative Conjunctions: Pairs in Harmony
explanation: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs (both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also). Ensure parallel grammatical structures after each part.
exampleText:
• both...and: She is both intelligent and hard-working.
• either...or: You can either choose the red coat or the blue jacket.

title: Lesson 64 — Conjunctions of Contrast: Although vs Despite
explanation: Although, even though, and though take a full clause (subject + verb). Despite and in spite of take a noun phrase or gerund (-ing).
exampleText:

• Despite / In spite of (+ noun phrase or gerund): Despite the heavy rain, they arrived at the concert on time.

title: Lesson 65 — Conjunctions of Purpose & Result: So That & In Order To

title: Lesson 66 — Sentence Connectors: However, Furthermore, Therefore
explanation: Transition words connect ideas between separate sentences. Place a semicolon or period before them and a comma immediately after.
exampleText:

title: Lesson 67 — Mastering Conjunctions for Cohesive Speech

title: Lesson 68 — Prepositions of Time: In, On, At Detailed Rules
explanation: Use 'at' for specific times/moments (at 5 PM, at noon), 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on May 1st), and 'in' for longer periods (in July, in 2024, in the morning).
exampleText:

title: Lesson 69 — Prepositions of Place: In, On, At Spatial Concepts
explanation: Use 'at' for specific points or locations (at the door), 'on' for surfaces (on the table), and 'in' for enclosed spaces or areas (in the room, in London).
exampleText:

title: Lesson 70 — Prepositions of Movement: Into, Onto, Through, Across

exampleText:

title: Lesson 71 — Dependent Prepositions with Popular Adjectives

title: Lesson 75 — Prepositional Phrases with 'On': On Time vs On Purpose

title: Lesson 76 — Prepositional Phrases with 'By': Transportation & Accident

title: Lesson 77 — Prepositions 'Under' & 'Over' in Idiomatic Phrases

title: Lesson 80 — Prepositions Following Nouns (Reason for, Solution to)

title: Lesson 87 — Borrow vs Lend vs Keep
explanation: 'Borrow' means to take temporarily ('Can I borrow your pen?'). 'Lend' means to give temporarily ('I will lend you my book'). 'Keep' means to hold permanently or long-term.

title: Lesson 88 — Rob vs Steal

title: Lesson 89 — Study vs Learn vs Teach
explanation: 'Study' is the process of reading/practicing. 'Learn' is acquiring knowledge or skill. 'Teach' is imparting knowledge to others.
exampleText:

title: Lesson 90 — Rise vs Raise vs Arise
explanation: 'Rise' is intransitive (no direct object: 'Prices rise'). 'Raise' is transitive (takes an object: 'Raise your hand'). 'Arise' means to come into notice or happen.
exampleText:
• Rise (intransitive: go up by itself): The sun rises in the east every morning.
• Raise (transitive: lift or increase something): Please raise your hand if you have a question.
• Arise (happen or come into notice): If any unexpected problems arise, let me know immediately.

title: Lesson 91 — Lie vs Lay vs Lain
explanation: 'Lie' means to recline or rest (intransitive: 'Lie down'). 'Lay' means to place something down (transitive: 'Lay the book on the table'). Past tense of lie is lay; past of lay is laid.
exampleText:
• Lie (recline / rest - intransitive): I like to lie on the couch and listen to music.
• Lay (place something down - transitive): Please lay the books gently on the wooden desk.
• Past Tense of Lie (lay): Yesterday, he lay on the grass for an hour.

title: Lesson 92 — Say vs Tell vs Speak vs Talk
explanation: Use 'tell' with a personal object ('Tell me the story'). Use 'say' without a personal object ('Say hello'). Use 'speak/talk' for languages or general dialogue.
exampleText:
• Say (without personal object): She said that she would arrive by noon.
• Tell (with personal object): He told me the good news right away.

title: Lesson 93 — Hear vs Listen
explanation: 'Hear' is passive perception of sound. 'Listen' is active, focused attention (requires 'to': 'Listen to the music').
exampleText:

• Listen (active focused attention with 'to'): Listen carefully to the instructions before starting.

title: Lesson 94 — See vs Look vs Watch
explanation: 'See' is automatic visual perception. 'Look' is directing your eyes at something ('Look at this'). 'Watch' is paying attention to something moving over time.
exampleText:
• See (automatic visual perception): I saw an old friend at the supermarket.
• Look (directing eyes with 'at'): Look at this beautiful sunset over the mountains!
• Watch (paying attention to movement over time): We watched a fascinating documentary last night.

title: Lesson 95 — Make vs Do
explanation: Use 'do' for actions, obligations, jobs, and repetitive tasks ('do homework, do research'). Use 'make' for creating, producing, or causing results ('make dinner, make mistakes').
exampleText:

• Make (creating, producing, causing results): She made a delicious dinner and made a great decision.

title: Lesson 96 — Bring vs Take vs Fetch
explanation: 'Bring' is movement toward the speaker ('Bring it here'). 'Take' is movement away from the speaker ('Take this to him'). 'Fetch' is going, getting, and returning.
exampleText:

• Take (movement away from speaker): Take these documents to the accounting department.

title: Lesson 97 — Come vs Go
explanation: 'Come' indicates movement toward the speaker or listener's location. 'Go' indicates movement away from the current location.
exampleText:

title: Lesson 98 — Remember vs Remind

title: Lesson 99 — Advise vs Advice
explanation: 'Advise' is the verb (pronounced /ədˈvaɪz/). 'Advice' is the uncountable noun (pronounced /ədˈvaɪs/).
exampleText:

title: Lesson 100 — Effect vs Affect
explanation: 'Affect' is usually a verb meaning to influence. 'Effect' is usually a noun meaning a result or consequence.
exampleText:

title: Lesson 101 — Accept vs Except
explanation: 'Accept' is a verb meaning to receive or agree to. 'Except' is a preposition meaning excluding.

• Except (preposition: excluding): Everyone arrived on time for the meeting except for Mark.

title: Lesson 102 — Loose vs Lose
explanation: 'Loose' is an adjective meaning not tight. 'Lose' is a verb meaning to misplace something or fail to win.
exampleText:

• Lose (verb: misplace or fail to win): Be careful not to lose your passport at the airport.
speechPrompt: This coat is very loose on me.

title: Lesson 103 — Everyday vs Every day
explanation: 'Everyday' (one word) is an adjective meaning ordinary or daily ('everyday clothes'). 'Every day' (two words) is an adverbial phrase meaning each day.
exampleText:
• Everyday (adjective: ordinary / routine): These are my everyday shoes for walking in the neighborhood.
• Every day (adverbial phrase: each day): I practice speaking English every day for thirty minutes.
speechPrompt: Stress has become part of everyday life.

title: Lesson 104 — Then vs Than
explanation: 'Then' refers to time, sequence, or consequence ('Do this, then that'). 'Than' is used exclusively in comparisons ('He is taller than me').
exampleText:
• Then (time, sequence, or consequence): We went to dinner, and then we watched a movie.
• Than (comparison): She is taller than her elder brother.
speechPrompt: We ate dinner and then went for a walk.

title: Lesson 105 — Their vs There vs They're
explanation: 'Their' shows possession ('their car'). 'There' indicates place or existence ('over there'). 'They're' is the contraction for 'they are'.
exampleText:
• Their (possessive pronoun): The students forgot their textbooks in the classroom.
• There (location / existence): There is a quiet park right around the corner.
• They're (contraction for 'they are'): They're planning to visit us during the winter holidays.
speechPrompt: The students forgot their textbooks.

title: Lesson 106 — Its vs It's
explanation: 'Its' is the possessive form ('The dog wagged its tail'). 'It's' is the contraction for 'it is' or 'it has'.
exampleText:
• Its (possessive form): The puppy wagged its tail happily.
• It's (contraction for 'it is' / 'it has'): It's going to be a sunny day today.
speechPrompt: The company updated its privacy policy.

title: Lesson 107 — Your vs You're
explanation: 'Your' is a possessive pronoun ('your hat'). 'You're' is the contraction for 'you are'.
exampleText:
• Your (possessive pronoun): Is this your laptop on the table?
• You're (contraction for 'you are'): You're going to do fantastic on the exam!
speechPrompt: Is this your umbrella left on the chair?

title: Lesson 108 — Whose vs Who's
explanation: 'Whose' shows possession ('Whose phone is ringing?'). 'Who's' is the contraction for 'who is' or 'who has'.
exampleText:
• Whose (possessive form): Whose coat is left hanging on the chair?
• Who's (contraction for 'who is' / 'who has'): Who's coming to the dinner party tonight?

title: Lesson 109 — Stationary vs Stationery
explanation: 'Stationary' means standing still or not moving. 'Stationery' refers to writing materials like paper and envelopes.

• Stationery (writing paper and envelopes): She bought elegant personalized stationery for writing letters.

title: Lesson 110 — Principal vs Principle
explanation: 'Principal' means chief/main or a school head. 'Principle' refers to a fundamental rule, truth, or moral value.
exampleText:
• Principal (chief / school head / main): The school principal delivered an inspiring speech.
• Principle (fundamental rule or moral value): He refuses to compromise on his core principles.
speechPrompt: Mr. Davis is the principal of our high school.

title: Lesson 111 — Beside vs Besides
explanation: 'Beside' means by the side of or next to. 'Besides' means in addition to or moreover.
exampleText:

• Besides (in addition to / moreover): Besides English, she speaks Spanish and French.
speechPrompt: Besides reading, I enjoy cooking and painting.

title: Lesson 112 — Among vs Between
explanation: Use 'between' when referring to distinct, individual items (usually two). Use 'among' when referring to a group or collective body of three or more.
exampleText:
• Between (distinct individual items / usually two): Choose between the blue shirt and the white one.
• Among (group or collective body of three or more): The treasure was divided among the four sailors.
speechPrompt: There is a secret agreement between the two directors.

title: Lesson 113 — Sometime vs Sometimes vs Some time
explanation: 'Sometime' means at an unspecified time. 'Sometimes' means occasionally. 'Some time' means a span of time.
exampleText:

• Sometimes (occasionally / at times): Sometimes I prefer staying home rather than going out.
• Some time (a period or duration of time): I need some time to think about your proposal.

title: Lesson 114 — Altogether vs All together
explanation: 'Altogether' means completely or entirely. 'All together' means gathered in one place as a group.
exampleText:

• All together (gathered in one place as a group): Let's sing the chorus all together now!
speechPrompt: We stood all together for the group photograph.

title: Lesson 115 — Compliment vs Complement
explanation: 'Compliment' means praise or admiration. 'Complement' means to complete or go well together with.
exampleText:
• Compliment (praise or admiration): He paid her a lovely compliment on her artwork.
• Complement (to complete or pair well with): The red wine complements the steak perfectly.
speechPrompt: She paid me a nice compliment on my speech.

title: Lesson 116 — Emigrate vs Immigrate
explanation: 'Emigrate' means to leave one's home country. 'Immigrate' means to move into a new country to live permanently.
exampleText:
• Emigrate (leave home country): My ancestors emigrated from Italy in 1910.
• Immigrate (move into new country permanently): They immigrated to Canada to start a new business.
speechPrompt: My grandparents immigrated to America eighty years ago.

title: Lesson 117 — Historic vs Historical
explanation: 'Historic' means famous, important, or monumental in history. 'Historical' means related to the study or facts of history.
exampleText:
• Historic (famous / important in history): Today is a historic moment for space exploration.
• Historical (related to facts/study of history): She loves reading historical fiction novels.
speechPrompt: She loves reading historical novels set in the 18th century.

title: Lesson 118 — Economic vs Economical
explanation: 'Economic' relates to the economy, finance, or trade. 'Economical' means thrifty, inexpensive, or avoiding waste.
exampleText:
• Economic (relating to economy / finance): The government introduced new economic reforms.
• Economical (thrifty / inexpensive / avoiding waste): Driving a hybrid car is very economical on fuel.
speechPrompt: The government announced new economic policies today.

title: Lesson 119 — Sensible vs Sensitive
explanation: 'Sensible' means reasonable, practical, or wise. 'Sensitive' means easily hurt, empathetic, or delicate.
exampleText:
• Sensible (reasonable / practical / wise): It is sensible to save money for emergency expenses.
• Sensitive (easily hurt / empathetic / delicate): Be careful what you say; he is very sensitive to criticism.
speechPrompt: She is very sensitive to loud noises and bright lights.

title: Lesson 120 — Desert vs Dessert
explanation: 'Desert' (stress on first syllable) is an arid land; as a verb, it means to abandon. 'Dessert' (stress on second syllable) is a sweet dish.
exampleText:
• Desert (arid dry land / abandon): Camels can survive in the harsh desert environment.
• Dessert (sweet dish after a meal): We ordered chocolate lava cake for dessert.
speechPrompt: Camels can travel long distances across the desert.

title: Lesson 121 — Quiet vs Quite vs Quit
explanation: 'Quiet' means silent/peaceful. 'Quite' means fairly, completely, or very. 'Quit' means to stop or leave.
exampleText:
• Quiet (silent / low noise): Please be quiet while the test is in progress.
• Quite (fairly / completely): It was quite cold outside yesterday evening.
• Quit (stop / resign): He decided to quit smoking for his health.
speechPrompt: The news was quite unexpected and surprising.

title: Lesson 122 — Capital vs Capitol
explanation: 'Capital' refers to a chief city, uppercase letter, or financial wealth. 'Capitol' specifically refers to a building housing a legislature.
exampleText:
• Capital (chief city / wealth / uppercase): Paris is the capital of France, and start your name with a capital letter.
• Capitol (legislative building): The congress met inside the state capitol building.
speechPrompt: The senators gathered inside the Capitol building.

title: Lesson 123 — Continuous vs Continual
explanation: 'Continuous' means unbroken without any interruption. 'Continual' means occurring repeatedly over time with short breaks.
exampleText:
• Continuous (unbroken without interruption): The rainfall was continuous for five full hours.
• Continual (occurring repeatedly with breaks): He suffered from continual interruptions throughout the workday.
speechPrompt: His continual interruptions disturbed the whole presentation.

title: Lesson 124 — Farther vs Further
explanation: 'Farther' refers to measurable physical distance. 'Further' refers to figurative distance, degree, or additional information.
exampleText:
• Farther (measurable physical distance): He can run farther down the track than I can.
• Further (figurative degree / additional info): Please contact our support office for further information.
speechPrompt: How much farther is it to the top of the hill?

title: Lesson 125 — Fewer vs Less
explanation: Use 'fewer' with plural countable nouns ('fewer books'). Use 'less' with singular uncountable nouns ('less sugar').
exampleText:
• Fewer (for plural countable nouns): There were fewer attendees at the meeting today than yesterday.
• Less (for singular uncountable nouns): Please add less sugar to my iced tea.
speechPrompt: Please add less sugar to my tea.

title: Lesson 126 — Number vs Amount
explanation: Use 'number' with countable nouns ('a number of cars'). Use 'amount' with uncountable nouns ('an amount of money').
exampleText:
• Number (for countable nouns): A large number of students attended the seminar.
• Amount (for uncountable nouns): They spent a significant amount of money on renovations.
speechPrompt: A significant amount of water was wasted.

title: Lesson 127 — Uninterested vs Disinterested
explanation: 'Uninterested' means not interested or bored. 'Disinterested' means impartial, unbiased, or neutral.
exampleText:
• Uninterested (not interested / bored): He seemed completely uninterested in watching the game.
• Disinterested (impartial / unbiased): A judge must remain a disinterested party in court.
speechPrompt: He seemed totally uninterested in the conversation.

title: Lesson 128 — Person vs People vs Persons vs Peoples
explanation: 'Person' is singular. 'People' is plural for human beings. 'Persons' is formal legal usage. 'Peoples' refers to distinct ethnic groups or nations.
exampleText:
• Person (singular individual): One person left their umbrella in the hallway.
• People (plural human beings): Many people enjoy traveling during the summer.
• Persons (formal legal usage): Authorized persons only are permitted past this door.
• Peoples (distinct ethnic groups/nations): The indigenous peoples of North America have rich heritage.
speechPrompt: She is a kind and thoughtful person.

title: Lesson 129 — Mastering Commonly Confused Words in Context

exampleText:

title: Lesson 130 — Subject vs Object Pronouns Rules
explanation: Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) as the doer of the verb. Use object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) after verbs and prepositions.
exampleText:
• Subject Pronoun (I, he, she, we, they): She and I completed the project ahead of schedule.
• Object Pronoun (me, him, her, us, them): The manager invited him and me to present the findings.

title: Lesson 131 — Possessive Adjectives vs Possessive Pronouns
explanation: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, our, their) come before nouns. Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) stand alone.
exampleText:
• Possessive Adjective (my, your, his, her, our, their + Noun): This is my jacket on the coat rack.
• Possessive Pronoun (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs): That blue umbrella over there is mine.
speechPrompt: Is this your notebook on the desk?

title: Lesson 132 — Reflexive & Emphatic Pronouns (Myself, Yourself)
explanation: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object are the same person ('I hurt myself'). Use emphatic pronouns to add emphasis ('I completed it myself').
exampleText:
• Reflexive Pronoun (Subject = Object): He accidentally cut himself while slicing vegetables.
• Emphatic Pronoun (Adding Emphasis): The president himself delivered the opening address.
speechPrompt: She looked at herself in the mirror.

title: Lesson 133 — Relative Pronouns: Who, Whom, Whose, Which, That
explanation: Use 'who' for people (subject), 'whom' for people (object), 'whose' for possession, 'which' for things, and 'that' for essential clauses.
exampleText:
• Who (subject for people): The artist who painted this mural lives in Chicago.
• Whom (object for people - formal): To whom should I direct this inquiry?
• Whose (possessive for people/things): I met a writer whose book became a bestseller.
• Which (non-essential information for things): My laptop, which I bought last year, is working great.
• That (essential clause for people/things): The document that you requested is attached.
speechPrompt: This is the camera that I bought last week.

title: Lesson 134 — Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clauses
explanation: Defining clauses provide essential information (no commas). Non-defining clauses add extra details (separated by commas, 'which' or 'who', never 'that').
exampleText:
• Defining Relative Clause (Essential - No Commas): The doctor who treated my knee was very kind.
• Non-Defining Relative Clause (Extra Details - With Commas): My brother, who lives in Seattle, is visiting us next week.
speechPrompt: The book that you recommended was brilliant.

title: Lesson 135 — Indefinite Pronouns: Someone, Anybody, Nothing, Everyone
explanation: Indefinite pronouns refer to non-specific people or things. They take singular verbs ('Everyone is ready', NOT 'Everyone are ready').
exampleText:
• Someone / Somebody (affirmative context): Someone left a notebook on the library desk.
• Anyone / Anybody (negative/question context): Did anybody call while I was out of the office?
• Everyone / Everybody (singular verb for all): Everyone is excited about the company retreat.
• Nothing / Nobody (negative meaning): Nothing is impossible if you work hard.

title: Lesson 136 — Demonstrative Pronouns: This, That, These, Those
explanation: Use 'this/these' for things near in time/space, and 'that/those' for distant things. Ensure singular/plural agreement with following verbs.
exampleText:
• This / These (Near in space or present time): This book in my hand is fascinating, and these shoes are comfortable.
• That / Those (Distant in space or past/future time): That car parked over there is electric, and those days were wonderful.
speechPrompt: That was a fantastic performance last night.

title: Lesson 137 — Reciprocal Pronouns: Each other vs One another
explanation: Use 'each other' typically for two subjects, and 'one another' for three or more. Both express mutual action.
exampleText:
• Each other (Mutual action between two subjects): The two brothers always support each other.
• One another (Mutual action among three or more): Team members should communicate openly with one another.
speechPrompt: Team members supported one another throughout the project.

title: Lesson 138 — Dummy Subject Pronouns: 'It' and 'There'
explanation: Use 'it' for weather, time, distance, and identification ('It is raining'). Use 'there' to state existence ('There are three reasons').
exampleText:
• Dummy Subject 'It' (weather / time / distance): It is six o'clock, and it is starting to snow outside.
• Dummy Subject 'There' (existence of items): There are three reasons why we chose this plan.

title: Lesson 139 — Common Pronoun Mistakes in Spoken Sentences
explanation: Avoid saying 'Me and John went' (correct: 'John and I went') or 'Between you and I' (correct: 'Between you and me').

• Correct: John and I (Subject): John and I went to the conference together.
• Correct: John and me (Object): The director greeted John and me warmly.
• Correct: Reflexive self (himself/myself): He completed the entire repair himself.

title: Lesson 140 — Gerunds vs Infinitives: Enjoy swimming vs Want to swim
explanation: Some verbs take a gerund (-ing) as an object (enjoy, avoid, suggest, consider). Other verbs take an infinitive (want, decide, hope, plan).

• Gerund after certain verbs (enjoy + -ing): I enjoy swimming in the ocean on warm summer days.
• Infinitive after certain verbs (want + to verb): I want to learn how to play the guitar.

title: Lesson 141 — Verbs Changing Meaning with Gerund or Infinitive
explanation: Verbs like 'stop', 'remember', and 'forget' change meaning: 'stop to smoke' (pause in order to smoke) vs 'stop smoking' (quit the habit).
exampleText:
• stop to do (pause in order to do something): He stopped to buy a newspaper on his way home.

• remember doing (past memory): I distinctly remember locking the front door.

title: Lesson 142 — Adjectives Ending in '-ed' vs '-ing'
explanation: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels ('I am bored'). -ing adjectives describe the thing/situation causing the feeling ('The class is boring').

title: Lesson 147 — Indefinite Articles 'A' & 'An' Phonetic Rules
explanation: Use 'a' before consonant sounds ('a university', 'a European') and 'an' before vowel sounds ('an hour', 'an honest person'). Base choice on sound, not spelling.

title: Lesson 148 — Definite Article 'The' Essential Guidelines
explanation: Use 'the' when referring to specific items known to speaker and listener, unique things (the sun, the world), or superlatives (the best).
exampleText:

• the (unique world objects / superlatives): The sun sets in the west; it is the tallest building.

title: Lesson 149 — Zero Article: When NOT to Use Articles
explanation: Do NOT use articles before general plural nouns, uncountable abstract concepts, names of languages, academic subjects, or meals.

• Zero Article (languages / academic subjects): She excels at mathematics and speaks fluent Italian.

title: Lesson 150 — Quantifiers: 'Some' vs 'Any' Rules
explanation: Use 'some' in positive affirmative sentences and polite offers/requests ('Would you like some tea?'). Use 'any' in negative sentences and general questions.
exampleText:
• some (affirmative statements & polite offers): I bought some fresh apples. Would you like some tea?
• any (negative statements & general questions): I don't have any questions. Do you have any milk left?
speechPrompt: I bought some fresh apples at the market.

title: Lesson 151 — Quantifiers: 'Much', 'Many', & 'A Lot Of'
explanation: Use 'many' with countable nouns, 'much' with uncountable nouns (mostly in questions/negatives), and 'a lot of' with both in affirmative statements.
exampleText:
• many (countable nouns): There aren't many open seats left in the auditorium.
• much (uncountable nouns in questions/negatives): How much free time do you have this afternoon?
• a lot of (both countable & uncountable): She has a lot of friends and a lot of confidence.
speechPrompt: How much time do we have before departure?

title: Lesson 152 — Quantifiers: 'Few' vs 'A Few' & 'Little' vs 'A Little'
explanation: 'A few' (countable) and 'a little' (uncountable) mean 'a small positive amount'. 'Few' and 'little' without 'a' have negative connotations meaning 'almost none'.
exampleText:
• a few (small positive amount - countable): I have a few friends coming over tonight.
• few (almost none - negative connotation): Regrettably, few people attended the morning lecture.
• a little (small positive amount - uncountable): I need a little help with this math problem.
• little (almost none - negative connotation): We have little hope of reaching the station on time.
speechPrompt: There is little water left in the jug.

title: Lesson 153 — Determiners: 'Each' vs 'Every'
explanation: 'Each' considers items individually (usually two or more). 'Every' considers items collectively as a group (three or more). Both take singular verbs.
exampleText:
• Each (individual focus / two or more): Each student received an award individually.
• Every (group collective focus / three or more): Every employee in the company attended the meeting.
speechPrompt: Every employee must attend the quarterly meeting.

title: Lesson 154 — Determiners: 'Both', 'Either', & 'Neither'
explanation: Use 'both' for two items together (plural verb). Use 'either' (one or the other) and 'neither' (not one nor the other) with singular verbs.
exampleText:
• Both (two items together - plural verb): Both candidates are highly qualified for the position.
• Either (one or the other - singular verb): You can choose either candidate for the interview.
• Neither (not one nor the other - singular verb): Neither answer is completely correct.
speechPrompt: Both of my brothers live in Sydney.

title: Lesson 155 — Determiners: 'All', 'Most', 'Whole', & 'No'
explanation: Use 'all' with plural/uncountable nouns, 'whole' with singular countable nouns ('the whole day'), and 'no' before nouns to express zero quantity.
exampleText:
• All (plural or uncountable nouns): All students must submit their assignments today.
• Whole (entire singular countable noun): I spent the whole day reading a captivating book.
• No (zero quantity before noun): There is no water left in the jug.
speechPrompt: All students must submit their work today.

title: Lesson 156 — Articles with Geographical Names & Places
explanation: Use 'the' with oceans, rivers, mountain ranges, desert regions, and plural country names (the USA, the Netherlands). Omit articles for single mountains, lakes, or most countries.
exampleText:
• the (oceans, rivers, mountain ranges, plural countries): The Amazon River flows into the Atlantic Ocean near the USA.
• Zero Article (single lakes, single mountains, most countries): Mount Everest is located in Nepal near Lake Baikal.

title: Lesson 157 — Mastering Articles & Quantifiers in Fast Speech

title: Lesson 158 — Capitalization Rules in Written English
explanation: Capitalize proper nouns, days of the week, months, holidays, titles, national adjectives, and the first word of every sentence.
exampleText:
• Proper Nouns & Names: Dr. Sarah Jenkins lives in London, England.
• Days, Months & Holidays: We are celebrating Thanksgiving on Thursday in November.
• Nationalities & Languages: He is studying Japanese literature and culture.
speechPrompt: English and Spanish are widely spoken.

title: Lesson 159 — Comma Rules: Separating Clauses & Lists
explanation: Use commas to separate items in a series, after introductory clauses, and before coordinating conjunctions connecting independent clauses.
exampleText:
• Items in a Series / List: We bought fresh apples, oranges, bananas, and grapes.
• Introductory Clause Separation: Although it was raining, we enjoyed our morning walk.
• Coordinating Conjunction Clause Connection: She wanted to go to the beach, but he preferred the mountains.
speechPrompt: I bought apples, bananas, and oranges.

title: Lesson 160 — Apostrophe Rules: Possessives vs Contractions
explanation: Use apostrophes for contractions (it's = it is) and possessives (dog's bone). Plural possessives place the apostrophe after the 's' (teachers' lounge).

explanation: Use strong past tense action verbs for achievements ('managed', 'implemented', 'orchestrated') and avoid overly tentative language.
exampleText:

title: Lesson 215 — Spoken vs Written English Grammar Conventions
explanation: Recognize when informal contractions and reduced forms are acceptable (spoken/casual text) versus when full forms are required (formal writing).
exampleText:
• Spoken English Convention (Contractions Acceptable): I'm gonna give it a try when I'm ready.
• Written English Convention (Full Forms Required): I am going to give it an attempt when I am ready.

title: Lesson 218 — Idioms for Emotions: Happiness, Anger & Stress
explanation: Learn expressive idioms: 'on cloud nine' (ecstatically happy), 'see red' (become furious), 'under the weather' (slightly unwell), 'over the moon' (delighted).
exampleText:
• Happiness: on cloud nine: She was on cloud nine after receiving her promotion.
• Anger: see red: He saw red when he noticed the damaged car.
• Stress: under the weather: I am feeling a bit under the weather today.
speechPrompt: I am feeling a bit under the weather today.

title: Lesson 219 — Idioms for Work, Success & Perseverance
explanation: Learn workplace idioms: 'hit the ground running' (start with immediate energy), 'learn the ropes' (master new tasks), 'burn the midnight oil' (work late into night).
exampleText:
• hit the ground running (start with energy): The new marketing director hit the ground running on day one.
• learn the ropes (master new skills): It takes a few weeks to learn the ropes in a new company.
• burn the midnight oil (work late): We had to burn the midnight oil to finish the proposal.
speechPrompt: We had to burn the midnight oil to meet the deadline.
optionsString: learn the ropes,burn the midnight oil,hit the ground running,cut corners

title: Lesson 220 — Idioms for Money, Decisions & Opportunities
explanation: Learn decision idioms: 'at a crossroads' (facing a big choice), 'break the bank' (cost too much), 'bite the bullet' (face a tough situation bravely).
exampleText:
• at a crossroads (facing a big decision): After graduating, she felt she was at a crossroads in life.
• break the bank (cost too much): Eating healthy meals at home won't break the bank.
• bite the bullet (face tough situation bravely): I decided to bite the bullet and go to the dentist.
speechPrompt: This vacation won't break the bank.
optionsString: bite the bullet,break the bank,at a crossroads,cost an arm and a leg

title: Lesson 221 — Descriptive Adjectives for Character & Personality
explanation: Expand personality vocabulary: meticulous (paying great attention to detail), charismatic (inspiring charm), compassionate (kind/empathetic), reliable (trustworthy).
exampleText:
• Meticulous (paying great attention to detail): She is a meticulous researcher who checks every fact twice.
• Charismatic (inspiring charm and devotion): The charismatic leader captivated the entire audience.
• Reliable (trustworthy and dependable): He is a reliable friend who is always there when needed.
speechPrompt: He is a compassionate and reliable friend.

title: Lesson 222 — Descriptive Vocabulary for Atmosphere & Settings
explanation: Describe places vividly: tranquil (peaceful/calm), bustling (full of noisy activity), picturesque (charming like a picture), vibrant (energetic/colorful).
exampleText:
• Tranquil (peaceful and calm): We spent a tranquil afternoon sitting beside the mountain lake.
• Bustling (full of energetic activity): The bustling street market was crowded with shoppers.
• Picturesque (charming like a picture): They visited a picturesque village nestled in the green hills.
speechPrompt: The bustling city market was filled with vivid colors.

title: Lesson 223 — Strong Verbs vs Weak Verbs with 'Very'
explanation: Upgrade your vocabulary by replacing 'very + weak verb/adjective': 'very tired' -> 'exhausted'; 'very clean' -> 'spotless'; 'very cold' -> 'freezing'; 'very smart' -> 'brilliant'.
exampleText:
• Upgrade: 'very tired' -> 'exhausted': After running the marathon, he felt completely exhausted.
• Upgrade: 'very clean' -> 'spotless': The kitchen counter was so clean it was spotless.
• Upgrade: 'very cold' -> 'freezing': Put on your thick coat; it is freezing outside!
• Upgrade: 'very smart' -> 'brilliant': She came up with a brilliant idea during the brainstorming session.
speechPrompt: The kitchen was sparkling and spotless.

title: Lesson 224 — Collocations with 'Take', 'Have', & 'Make'
explanation: Natural verb-noun pairings: take a break, take a risk, have a conversation, have an impact, make progress, make an effort.
exampleText:
• Collocations with 'Take' (take a break / risk): Let's take a short ten-minute break before continuing.
• Collocations with 'Have' (have a chat / impact): We had an engaging conversation regarding the project.
• Collocations with 'Make' (make progress / effort): You have made significant progress in your English fluency.
speechPrompt: Let's take a quick fifteen-minute break.

title: Lesson 225 — Collocations with 'Do', 'Pay', & 'Keep'
explanation: Natural verb-noun pairings: do business, do a favor, pay attention, pay a compliment, keep a promise, keep in mind.
exampleText:
• Collocations with 'Do' (do business / a favor): Could you do me a quick favor and hold this door?
• Collocations with 'Pay' (pay attention / compliment): Please pay close attention to the safety instructions.
• Collocations with 'Keep' (keep a promise / in mind): Keep in mind that the office is closed on holidays.
speechPrompt: You should pay close attention to the instructions.
optionsString: keep in mind,pay attention,do a favor,keep a promise

title: Lesson 226 — Expressing Sympathy, Congratulations & Praise
explanation: Conversational phrases: 'I am so sorry for your loss', 'Warmest congratulations on your achievement!', 'Kudos to you for a job well done!'
exampleText:
• Expressing Sympathy: I am so deeply sorry to hear about your loss.
• Expressing Congratulations: Warmest congratulations on winning first place!
• Expressing Praise: Kudos to you and your team for a job exceptionally well done!
speechPrompt: I am so sorry to hear about your bad news.

title: Lesson 227 — Making Proposals, Suggestions & Recommendations
explanation: Use persuasive phrases: 'How about we try...?', 'I strongly recommend that we...', 'Why don't we consider...?', 'It might be beneficial to...'
exampleText:
• How about we try...?: How about we try holding the meeting online instead?
• I strongly recommend that...: I strongly recommend that we update our software immediately.
• Why don't we consider...?: Why don't we consider hiring a consultant for guidance?
speechPrompt: How about we schedule the meeting for Tuesday morning?
optionsString: strongly recommend,how about,why don't we,I suggest

title: Lesson 228 — Summarizing & Paraphrasing Ideas in Speaking
explanation: Useful transition phrases: 'To sum up...', 'In short...', 'To put it another way...', 'In essence, what I am saying is...'
exampleText:
• To sum up...: To sum up, our main priority is improving user experience.
• In short...: In short, we exceeded our sales targets for this quarter.
• To put it another way...: To put it another way, quality matters far more than quantity.

optionsString: To sum up,In short,In essence,To put it another way

title: Lesson 229 — Storytelling Techniques & Narrative Connectors
explanation: Engage listeners with narrative markers: 'It all started when...', 'Out of nowhere...', 'To make a long story short...', 'Before I knew it...'
exampleText:

title: Lesson 230 — Countable vs Uncountable Nouns & Tricky Nouns
explanation: Uncountable nouns (information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, news) never take 'a/an' and do not add '-s'. Use 'a piece of' to count them.
exampleText:
• Uncountable Noun Rule (No 'a/an' & No plural '-s'): She gave me valuable advice regarding my career path.
• Counting Phrase (a piece of / an item of): He carried three pieces of heavy luggage to the check-in desk.
speechPrompt: All the news was positive.

title: Lesson 231 — Plural Noun Rules & Irregular Plurals
explanation: Irregular plurals change vowels (man -> men, tooth -> teeth, mouse -> mice) or stay identical (sheep, deer, fish). Always-plural nouns take plural verbs (pants, scissors, glasses).
exampleText:
• Irregular Vowel Change Plurals (man->men, tooth->teeth): Both men and women participated in the community clean-up.
• Identical Singular & Plural (sheep, deer, fish): A flock of sheep was grazing peacefully on the hill.
• Always-Plural Nouns (glasses, scissors, pants): Where did I place my reading glasses and sharp scissors?
speechPrompt: The sheep were grazing peacefully in the field.

title: Lesson 232 — Compound Nouns & Possessive Nouns Rules
explanation: Possessive 's is used for people and animals ('John's car'). Use 'of' for inanimate objects ('the roof of the house'). Compound nouns form plurals on the head noun ('passers-by').
exampleText:
• Possessive 's for People & Animals: John's briefcase was left in the conference room.
• Possessive 'of' for Inanimate Objects: The roof of the historic house was damaged by storm.
• Compound Noun Plurals on Head Noun: Several passers-by helped push the stalled vehicle.
speechPrompt: They are my brother's close friends.
optionsString: roof of the house,house's roof,roof house,roofs house

title: Lesson 233 — Causative Verbs: Make, Have, Get, Let, & Help
explanation: Structure rules: Make/Have/Let + object + base verb ('She made me clean'); Get + object + to-infinitive ('I got him to repair the sink'); Help takes base verb or to-infinitive.
exampleText:
• Make (force / obligation + base verb): The teacher made all students rewrite their essays.
• Have (assign responsibility + base verb): I will have my assistant book your hotel room.
• Get (persuade / convince + to-infinitive): I managed to get the technician to repair my laptop.
• Let (allow / give permission + base verb): My parents let me borrow their car for the road trip.
• Help (assist + base verb or to-infinitive): She helped me carry the heavy boxes up the stairs.
speechPrompt: I will get the mechanic to check the brakes.
optionsString: made me rewrite,made me to rewrite,got me rewrite,let me to rewrite

title: Lesson 234 — Using 'Suggest' & 'Recommend' Correctly
explanation: Never say 'suggest me to do'. Correct structures: 'suggest + -ing' ('I suggest taking a break') OR 'suggest that + subject + base verb' ('I suggest that he take a break').
exampleText:
• Structure: suggest + -ing: I suggest taking a short fifteen-minute walk to clear your mind.
• Structure: suggest that + subject + base verb: I suggest that he review the financial document before submitting it.
• Structure: recommend that + subject + base verb: The doctor recommended that she rest for three full days.
speechPrompt: The doctor recommended that she rest for three days.
optionsString: taking,to take,that he takes,him to take
